title: Emergency Oral Schedule II Dispensing
topic: Controlled prescriptions / Emergency oral Schedule II
subtopic: The emergency gate, the record, and which follow-up clock controls
learning_objectives: Apply each sovereign's definition of an emergency situation, and notice that they are not the same test.

Trace why a Massachusetts emergency oral prescription runs on the ePrescribing-exception route rather than the two-day electronic clause, and how the regulation's seven business days sit beside the statute's 7 days.
Identify which follow-up period actually binds when both sovereigns reach the same prescription.
State what the pharmacist must write down, attach or annotate at each stage.
Name the consequence the regulation attaches to the pharmacist's own failure to notify the DEA.

orientation.text: Schedule II normally means a signed prescription before the drug leaves the shelf: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) lets a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II drug only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner, except as paragraph (d) provides. The emergency oral pathway is that exception, and it is built in three layers. The first is a gate, and each sovereign defines it differently. Federal law, in 21 CFR 290.10, requires the prescribing practitioner to determine that immediate administration is necessary, that no appropriate alternative treatment is available including a drug that is not in Schedule II, and that it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription before the dispensing. Massachusetts, in 105 CMR 721.010, asks whether immediate administration of the controlled substance is necessary and then either that it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an ELECTRONIC prescription before the dispensing or that the practitioner determines the electronic requirement would cause a delay adversely impacting the patient; it also takes in any other Emergency Situation the Commissioner defines in Department guidance. Massachusetts carries no no-alternative-treatment element at all.

On Massachusetts facts the two definitions are cumulative, because each sovereign conditions its own permission on its own test: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in an emergency situation as 290.10 defines it, and 105 CMR 721.060(B) lets a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II substance on the prescriber's authorization only in case of an Emergency Situation as 721.010 defines it. Facts that satisfy the Massachusetts definition but not the federal one leave the oral route closed: an appropriate non-Schedule II alternative defeats federal element (b), and a signed written prescription that could reach the pharmacy before the dispensing defeats element (c) even where an electronic prescription cannot be transmitted. The three federal elements are the prescribing practitioner's determination; the Massachusetts definition is written around the prescriber's circumstances and makes its delay limb the practitioner's determination. 105 CMR 721.070(C) spares a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid oral prescription from verifying that it properly falls under an ePrescribing exception, which is a question of Massachusetts exception status and does not supply a federal element the facts defeat.

Once both gates are passed the pharmacist may dispense on the oral authorization, but only the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, and, where the prescriber is not known to the pharmacist, only after a reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered individual practitioner, which Massachusetts states as a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization was issued by a prescribing practitioner. The prescription is immediately reduced to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature, and on Massachusetts facts with everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires, 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allowing it to be entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead of written out. Those Massachusetts duties are the statute's own, and s. 20 states them for any oral controlled-substance prescription rather than for the emergency alone. Section 20(a) directs the pharmacist, upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, to reduce it to writing immediately on a prescription form and to record an enumerated list of particulars, and s. 20(b) states the authentication duty separately: if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, the pharmacist shall make a reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner. The emergency regulation restates neither list. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) sends the record back to s. 20(a), and 721.060(B)(3) puts the good faith effort in its own words, so what the writing has to contain is fixed by the statute and not by the emergency paragraph. Massachusetts is explicit about what the emergency does and does not touch: 105 CMR 721.060(A) waives the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, and the written and oral prescriptions it then permits must comply with all other prescription requirements.

The third layer is the follow-up, and it is where candidates lose the question. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) opens with an ELECTRONIC follow-up within 2 days whenever a practitioner prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription, which is tempting to read as the stricter Massachusetts answer. That clause is the statute's rule for a practitioner who has received no exception from using an electronic prescription from the commissioner under s. 23(h); the same subsection sends a practitioner who has received one to a WRITTEN prescription within not more than 7 days, or such shorter period as federal law requires. Section 23(h) is where those exceptions come from: it directs the commissioner to establish them through regulation and limits them to a list that includes emergency situations, 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations accordingly, and 105 CMR 721.020(A) makes a 721.070 exception the only basis for a non-electronic prescription generated in the Commonwealth. A lawful Massachusetts emergency oral prescription is therefore always issued under an exception, and the 2-day clause is not the route it travels.

Where that leaves the count is worth stating plainly, because the Massachusetts texts do not use the same unit. The statute's exception route is not more than 7 days for a written follow-up. 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the emergency prescription to 105 CMR 721.070(B), which gives not more than seven business days for a written or electronic one, or such shorter period as federal law requires; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states seven business days directly for this pathway; and the Department's manual states seven business days for every oral schedule II through V prescription issued under an exception, the emergency included. The statute keys its 7-day route to a practitioner who has RECEIVED an exception, a phrase that fits the applied-for waiver most naturally and that the statute does not confine to waiver holders, so the emergency oral prescription reads onto the 7-day route while the regulation and the Department measure it in seven business days. For this prescription the difference changes nothing: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription, 721.070(B) yields in its own words to that shorter federal period, and seven days run out before seven business days do. Seven days from the oral authorization is the deadline that satisfies every period these texts state.

The record layer finishes the pathway. The prescriber writes on the face of the follow-up the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order, both of which 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires and the first of which 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) requires as well; on Massachusetts facts the follow-up also indicates that it is issued to document an oral prescription, which M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires of an electronic or written follow-up, 105 CMR 721.070(B) requires of a written one, and the Department's manual states for every emergency follow-up. The pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up to the writing made on the telephone and annotates the record of an electronic one with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. If no complying follow-up is delivered, the pharmacist notifies the nearest DEA office, and the pharmacist's own failure to notify voids the federal authority to have dispensed without a written prescription.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones at 7pm on a Friday from home. A patient needs morphine oral solution tonight; the prescriber tells you that no drug outside Schedule II would be an appropriate treatment, that the practice's e-prescribing system is down, and that there is no way to get a signed paper prescription to your pharmacy before the dose is needed. The prescriber is not known to you. How much may you dispense, and by when must the follow-up arrive?
steps: Work the federal gate first, because federal law opens no other oral route for a Schedule II drug. 21 CFR 290.10 needs all three of the prescriber's determinations: immediate administration is necessary, no appropriate alternative treatment is available including a drug outside Schedule II, and a written prescription cannot reasonably be provided before the dispensing. An e-prescribing outage on its own would not establish the third element; here the prescriber has also ruled out getting a signed paper prescription to you in time.

Work the Massachusetts gate. Immediate administration is necessary and it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an electronic prescription before the dispensing, so this is an Emergency Situation under 105 CMR 721.010. Both definitions are satisfied, and on Massachusetts facts both must be.
Because the prescriber is not known to you, make a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered prescribing practitioner before dispensing anything.

Limit the quantity to what is adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period. Anything beyond the emergency period needs a paper or electronic prescription signed by the practitioner, not this authorization.
Immediately reduce the oral prescription to writing, carrying every required element except the practitioner's signature.

Now pick the follow-up clock. The emergency is an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), one of those M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish, so the 2-day electronic clause that opens s. 20(c) is not the route. The statute's exception route states not more than 7 days; 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B) for not more than seven business days or such shorter period as federal law requires; and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states seven business days for this pathway directly.

Supply the federal period. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription. That matches the statute's 7 days and runs out before seven business days, so seven days from the oral authorization is the deadline every text accepts.
worked_examples.resolution: Dispense only the emergency-period quantity, after the reasonable good faith effort to identify the prescriber, reduce the order to writing immediately, and expect the follow-up within seven days of the oral authorization bearing Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, the date of the oral order, and the indication that it documents an oral prescription. Answering two days applies the statute's no-exception clause to a prescription issued under an exception; answering seven business days overlooks the shorter federal period that 721.070(B) defers to in its own words.

worked_examples.scenario: Eight days have passed since you dispensed on an emergency oral Schedule II authorization. You have telephoned the prescriber's office twice and documented both calls, and no written or electronic follow-up has arrived. A colleague says the documented calls discharge your duty. Is that right?
steps: The practitioner's 7-day federal period has expired, so the follow-up is missing rather than merely late.

Federal law places a duty on you at that point: notify the nearest office of the DEA that the practitioner failed to deliver the follow-up prescription. Chasing the prescriber is not the duty the regulation names, and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(5) places a matching duty on the pharmacist where the practitioner fails to deliver in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4).
Read the consequence attached to your own omission. Failure of the pharmacist to notify voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague is wrong. Documented calls do not substitute for the notification, and the consequence of skipping it falls on the dispensing itself: it loses the federal authority it rested on.

worked_examples.scenario: On a Wednesday afternoon a Massachusetts practice's e-prescribing system goes down. A prescriber telephones an oral order for a Schedule II opioid for a patient who needs a dose within the hour, and mentions that the patient's daughter is at the practice and could bring a signed paper prescription to your pharmacy in twenty minutes. Your technician says the outage makes this a Massachusetts Emergency Situation, so the telephone order can be dispensed. Is that right?
steps: Test the Massachusetts definition. Immediate administration is necessary and it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an electronic prescription before the dispensing, so the facts fit the Emergency Situation in 105 CMR 721.010.

Test the federal definition separately. 21 CFR 290.10(c) asks whether it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription to be presented before the dispensing. A signed paper prescription can be in your hands within the hour, so that element fails, and 290.10(b) would have to be satisfied as well.

Draw the consequence. Without a federal emergency situation the oral route in 21 CFR 1306.11(d) is closed and 1306.11(a) requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner; the Massachusetts permission in 105 CMR 721.060(B) is state law and supplies no federal element.

Take the signed paper prescription when it arrives. Massachusetts permits a written prescription where electronic prescribing is unavailable because of a temporary technological or electrical failure, and 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to carry the practitioner's signature and, since it is handed over rather than transmitted by facsimile, to be written on a tamper-resistant form.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The facts satisfy the Massachusetts definition but not the federal one, and on Massachusetts facts the oral Schedule II route needs both. The error the scenario invites is treating an electronic-prescribing outage as settling the federal question, which asks about a written prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Federal law adds one element to the emergency-situation test that Massachusetts does not state at all. Name it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: That no appropriate alternative treatment is available, including administration of a drug which is not a Schedule II controlled substance (21 CFR 290.10(b)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The federal emergency test turns on the impracticability of providing a ______ prescription; the Massachusetts test turns on the impracticability of generating or transmitting an ______ prescription.
A prescriber's facts satisfy 105 CMR 721.010 but not 21 CFR 290.10. May the pharmacist dispense the Schedule II drug on the oral authorization?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in a federal emergency situation, and 1306.11(a) otherwise requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner; the Massachusetts permission in 105 CMR 721.060(B) does not supply the missing federal element.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does the 2-day electronic follow-up that opens M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) NOT govern a Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because that clause is the statute's rule for a practitioner who has received no exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), and emergency situations are among the exceptions s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates; the statute's exception route states not more than 7 days, and 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states the follow-up as not more than seven business days, or ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: such shorter period as is required by federal law, which here is the 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4), counted from the practitioner's authorization of the emergency oral prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Federal law requires two things on the face of the follow-up prescription, and Massachusetts adds a third. Name all three.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order (21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4); the first is required by 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) as well), plus the indication that the prescription is issued to document an oral prescription (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c), 105 CMR 721.070(B) and the Department's manual).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What happens if the pharmacist does not notify the DEA when the follow-up never arrives?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The failure voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to have dispensed without a written prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A written follow-up arrives on an ordinary prescription pad. What is the format problem, and what does it mean for the emergency dispensing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires a written prescription, where state and federal law permit one, to carry the practitioner's signature and to be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid under 105 CMR 721.040(A), so it is not a follow-up delivered in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4), and the pharmacist's DEA-notification duty answers a failure to deliver one that complies.

quick_review.text: In a defined emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II substance on a practitioner's oral authorization, limited to the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, with a reasonable effort to identify a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.
Outside paragraph (d), 21 CFR 1306.11(a) permits a Schedule II drug to be dispensed only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner.

On Massachusetts facts both definitions must be satisfied: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in a 21 CFR 290.10 emergency situation, and 105 CMR 721.060(B) opens its route only in case of a 105 CMR 721.010 Emergency Situation.

The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allows entry into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead.

A Massachusetts Emergency Situation is itself an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), one of those M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish, which is why the follow-up runs on the exception route rather than the 2-day electronic clause.

105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the Massachusetts follow-up as seven business days after authorizing the emergency orally transmitted prescription, requires Authorization for Emergency Dispensing on its face, and requires it to comply with federal and state law; the Department's manual states the same seven business days.

The Massachusetts texts count differently: the statute's exception route is not more than 7 days for a written follow-up and the regulation not more than seven business days for a written or electronic one, so a follow-up delivered within 7 days meets both.

Federal law requires the follow-up within 7 days after the emergency oral authorization, and because 105 CMR 721.070(B) states its own period subject to any shorter federal one, seven days is the operative deadline.
If the follow-up does not arrive, the pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an ePrescribing exception or waiver.
A written follow-up must still satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and does not discharge the follow-up the practitioner owes.

decision_logic.condition: A practitioner offers an oral Schedule II authorization.
decision_logic.action: Work both definitions. The federal test in 21 CFR 290.10 adds a no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element and is keyed to a written prescription; the Massachusetts test in 105 CMR 721.010 is keyed to an electronic one and has a delay limb. On Massachusetts facts both must be satisfied before the oral route is open.

decision_logic.condition: The Massachusetts definition is satisfied but a federal element is not.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense on the oral authorization. 21 CFR 1306.11(a) requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner outside paragraph (d), and an ePrescribing exception may let the prescriber issue that written prescription in Massachusetts.

decision_logic.condition: Both definitions are satisfied and the practitioner is not known to you.
decision_logic.action: Make a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered prescribing practitioner, then dispense no more than the amount adequate for the emergency period.

decision_logic.condition: You have dispensed on the oral authorization.
decision_logic.action: Immediately reduce it to writing, or enter it into a compliant electronic pharmacy system as 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allows, carrying every required element except the practitioner's signature.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked how long the practitioner has to deliver the follow-up.
decision_logic.action: Do not reach for the 2-day clause: it is the statute's rule where the practitioner has received no s. 23(h) exception, and the emergency is one of those exceptions. The statute's exception route gives not more than 7 days, 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B) for seven business days or a shorter federal period, and 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) supplies 7 days from the oral authorization, which is the shortest of them.

decision_logic.condition: A written rather than electronic follow-up is used.
decision_logic.action: Check its face for Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, the date of the oral order and the indication that it documents an oral prescription; check the Massachusetts written-format requirements; and attach it to the oral prescription you reduced to writing.

decision_logic.condition: The follow-up arrives as an electronic prescription.
decision_logic.action: Annotate the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order rather than filing a printout against the attachment rule.

decision_logic.condition: The federal 7-day period has run with no complying follow-up delivered.
decision_logic.action: Notify the nearest DEA office of the practitioner's failure to deliver.

ma_vs_federal.text: The two definitions of an emergency situation are not the same test, and on Massachusetts facts both must be met; a fact pattern that satisfies 105 CMR 721.010 but not 21 CFR 290.10 does not open the oral Schedule II route.

Massachusetts frames the emergency as a waiver of the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, leaving every other prescription requirement in force; federal law frames it as the exception to the signed written prescription that 21 CFR 1306.11(a) otherwise requires.
The seven-business-day Massachusetts count is not extra time: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to any shorter period federal law requires, and the 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) is shorter.

Federal law splits the handling of the follow-up by medium, attaching a paper one and annotating the record of an electronic one; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(5) states the attachment step with no annotation counterpart.

exceptions.text: Dispensing beyond the emergency period is not covered by the oral authorization and requires a paper or electronic prescription signed by the practitioner.
A central fill pharmacy is not authorized to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or a practitioner.
Unlike the waiver route in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(3), which a practitioner applies for and receives, the emergency exception is not applied for; it attaches to the situation itself.
A mailed follow-up meets its period by the postmark rather than by the date the pharmacy receives it.

Outside the settings named in 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g), a faxed Schedule II prescription does not stand in for the original manually signed one, and both 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) provide for the written follow-up to be delivered in person or by mail.

timing_deadlines.event: Federal emergency oral Schedule II follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days after authorizing the emergency oral prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the shortest period reaching the prescription, so it is the operative deadline.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts regulation, follow-up under the ePrescribing exception route
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 business days, or such shorter period as federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.070(B) defers to the federal period rather than extending it, and the Department's manual states the same seven business days.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts regulation, emergency Schedule II follow-up stated directly
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 business days after authorizing the emergency orally transmitted prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the period for this pathway and requires the follow-up to comply with federal and state law.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts statute, written follow-up where the practitioner has received a commissioner's exception
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 days, or such shorter period as federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) counts 7 days where the regulation counts seven business days, so a follow-up delivered within 7 days meets both.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Once the federal period has run
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: No separate period; the consequence attaches to the omission
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authority to have dispensed without a written prescription is voided.

forms_records.text: The oral prescription is immediately reduced to writing with every element 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature; on Massachusetts facts it carries everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires and may be entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead of being written out.

What M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires on that writing is a list rather than a cross-reference: the name, address and registration number of the practitioner and the name of any expressly authorized representative, the date of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the serial number the dispensing pharmacy assigns, the name of that pharmacy, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Section 20(b) adds the reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner where that practitioner is not known to the pharmacist.
The follow-up bears the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order on its face.

On Massachusetts facts the follow-up also indicates that it is issued to document an oral prescription, which M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires of an electronic or written follow-up and 105 CMR 721.070(B) of a written one, and which the Department's manual states for every emergency follow-up.

On receipt the pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up to the oral prescription earlier reduced to writing, and annotates the record of an electronic follow-up with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.

A written follow-up must carry the practitioner's signature and satisfy 105 CMR 721.020(F), which governs written prescriptions where state and federal law permit them: transmitted by facsimile or similar technology, or written on a tamper-resistant form. Because 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) provide for the written prescription to be delivered in person or by mail, and because outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g) a faxed Schedule II prescription does not replace the original manually signed one, the tamper-resistant form is the route that fits this follow-up.

A prescription in a format that does not conform is invalid under 105 CMR 721.040(A), so it is not a follow-up delivered in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4), and the pharmacist's DEA-notification duty answers the practitioner's failure to deliver one that complies.

role_duties.duty: Determine the three federal emergency elements, act within the Massachusetts Emergency Situation, and cause the follow-up prescription bearing the required face notations to be delivered within the period.
Limit the quantity to the emergency period, make a reasonable effort to identify a prescriber who is not known to you, and reduce the order to writing immediately.
Notify the nearest DEA office when the follow-up is not delivered, understanding that omitting the notification voids the authority relied on to dispense.
Do not refuse an otherwise valid oral prescription for inability to confirm the practitioner's exception status; 105 CMR 721.070(C) imposes no such verification duty.

common_traps.text: Answering two days on a Massachusetts emergency oral question applies the statute's no-exception clause to a prescription that is always issued under an ePrescribing exception.
Answering seven business days treats the Massachusetts count as extra time, when 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to the shorter federal period.

Reading the Massachusetts gate as the whole test: the federal elements are separate, and an electronic-prescribing outage does not establish the federal element, which asks about a written prescription.
Carrying the federal no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element into the Massachusetts test, or the Massachusetts delay limb into the federal one, mixes two definitions that differ.
Knowing the DEA notification duty without its consequence leaves the candidate unable to say what turns on the pharmacist's omission.
Treating an emergency oral authorization as covering continued therapy overlooks that dispensing beyond the emergency period needs a signed prescription.
Refusing a prescription because the practitioner's exception status cannot be confirmed invents a verification duty the regulation does not impose on the pharmacist.
Naming two face items on Massachusetts facts drops the indication that the follow-up is issued to document an oral prescription.
Accepting a faxed copy as the delivered Schedule II follow-up overlooks that outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g) federal law looks for the original manually signed prescription.
